title: Comprehensions
summary: Build a new list, dict, or set from an existing one in a single readable line.

checkpoints.title: One line instead of a loop
checkpoints.content: A list comprehension `[x * 2 for x in nums]` builds a brand-new list by applying an expression to every item in `nums` — it's shorthand for a `for` loop that appends to an empty list. You can also filter with a trailing `if`: `[x for x in nums if x > 0]` keeps only the positive values.
checkpoints.explanation: Comprehensions don't do anything a loop can't — they're just a more compact, more Pythonic way to write the common 'build a new collection from an old one' pattern.

hints.H0: Read it right to left: the expression first, then where the items come from, then an optional filter.
hints.H1: `[x * 2 for x in nums]` means 'for each x in nums, put x * 2 in the new list'.
hints.H2: It's equivalent to: result = []; for x in nums: result.append(x * 2).

checkpoints.title: Predict a list comprehension's result
checkpoints.content: What does `[n * n for n in [1, 2, 3, 4]]` evaluate to?

options.explanation: Each item n is squared (n * n) and collected into the new list, in the same order.
That's the original list unchanged — the comprehension actually applies n * n to every item.
A list comprehension builds a list, not a single summed number — that would need sum() around it.

checkpoints.explanation: List comprehensions apply the leading expression to every item, producing a new list of the same length.

hints.H0: The expression before `for` is applied to every item.
hints.H1: n * n means each number gets squared.

checkpoints.title: Filter with a comprehension
checkpoints.content: Given `nums = [3, -1, 4, -2, 5]`, write a list comprehension that keeps only the positive numbers.
checkpoints.answer: [n for n in nums if n > 0]
checkpoints.explanation: The trailing `if n > 0` filters out any item that doesn't satisfy the condition before it's added to the new list.

hints.H0: Comprehensions support an optional `if` clause after the `for`.
hints.H1: The condition goes at the end: `for n in nums if <condition>`.
hints.H2: Use `[n for n in nums if n > 0]`.

checkpoints.title: Recognize a dict comprehension
checkpoints.content: Which expression builds a dictionary mapping each word in `words` to its length?

options.explanation: Curly braces with a key:value pair before the for clause build a dict comprehension — one entry per word.
Square brackets build a list, and a list can't hold key:value pairs this way — that syntax isn't valid Python.
That maps length to word instead — the key comes first, so this reverses which side is the key and which is the value.

checkpoints.explanation: A dict comprehension uses `{key_expr: value_expr for item in iterable}` — curly braces plus a colon-separated pair.

hints.H0: Dict comprehensions use curly braces, like a dict literal.
hints.H1: The part before the colon becomes the key; after the colon is the value.
hints.H2: Use {w: len(w) for w in words} to map each word to its length.
